---
title: "Writing your own AlphaSimR program"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4, dpi = 110)
```

`line_pipeline()` and `backcross_program()` are ready-made, but most real
questions need a scheme of your own. `alphasim_program()` turns any
[AlphaSimR](https://cran.r-project.org/package=AlphaSimR) script into
something tidyagsim can replicate, tune and compare. This article builds one
step by step. It starts from a plain AlphaSimR script and adds one
tidyagsim piece at a time, so you can see what each piece does for you.

If you have not used AlphaSimR before, its
[introductory vignette](https://cran.r-project.org/package=AlphaSimR/vignettes/intro.html)
explains founders, `SimParam`, crossing and selection. You only need the
basics here.

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(tidyagsim)
library(AlphaSimR)
library(ggplot2)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12))
```

## Who does what

AlphaSimR simulates the genetics: genomes, crosses, phenotypes and selection.
tidyagsim runs the *study* around it. You write the breeding scheme once, and
tidyagsim does the bookkeeping that turns it into a fair experiment.

| You write | tidyagsim does |
|---|---|
| One run of your breeding scheme, as a function | Builds new founders for every replicate, from its own seed |
| The settings you want to compare, marked with `tune()` | Runs every design on every replicate, with the same seeds (paired) |
| What to report at the end, as a named list | Collects the outcomes and summarizes them with standard errors |
| (Optional) `tracker$record()` calls each year | Turns the record into gain, gain per year, diversity, cost and trajectories |

## Step 1: a plain AlphaSimR script

Here is a small recurrent selection program in ordinary AlphaSimR. It makes
50 founders, then runs five cycles of phenotyping, selecting `n_select`
parents and crossing them.

```{r}
founder_haplotypes <- quickHaplo(nInd = 50, nChr = 5, segSites = 100, inbred = TRUE)
SP <- SimParam$new(founder_haplotypes)
SP$addTraitA(nQtlPerChr = 20)
SP$setVarE(h2 = 0.3)
founders <- newPop(founder_haplotypes)

pop <- founders
n_select <- 10
for (cycle in 1:5) {
  pop <- setPheno(pop)
  parents <- selectInd(pop, n_select)
  pop <- randCross(parents, nCrosses = 100)
}
mean(gv(pop)) - mean(gv(founders))
```

That is one run, with one setting, of one random founder population. To ask
"how many parents should I select?" you would need to rerun it many times for
each candidate, with fresh founders each time, keep the random numbers
comparable between candidates, and summarize. That bookkeeping is what
tidyagsim does.

## Step 2: make it a function

Wrap one run in a function. Three rules:

1. The first two arguments are `founders` (an AlphaSimR `Pop`) and `SP` (the
   `SimParam`). tidyagsim supplies both.
2. The other arguments are your design settings.
3. Return a named list of single numbers, the outcomes you want to compare.

```{r}
recurrent <- function(founders, SP, n_select, cycles = 5) {
  pop <- founders
  for (cycle in seq_len(cycles)) {
    pop <- setPheno(pop)
    parents <- selectInd(pop, n_select)
    pop <- randCross(parents, nCrosses = 100)
  }
  list(gain = (mean(gv(pop)) - mean(gv(founders))) / sd(gv(founders)))
}
```

Nothing tidyagsim-specific is inside yet. You can test it by calling it
directly with the founders from step 1:

```{r}
recurrent(founders, SP, n_select = 10)
```

Do **not** call `set.seed()` inside the function. tidyagsim seeds every
replicate itself, and that is how paired comparisons work.

## Step 3: turn it into a spec and replicate it

`alphasim_program()` takes the function, values for its settings, and a
founder recipe from `asr_founders()`. The recipe describes how to make
founders and the trait. It does not make them yet: every replicate makes its
own from its own seed.

```{r}
spec <- alphasim_program(
  recurrent,
  n_select = 10,
  founders = asr_founders(n_founders = 50, n_chr = 5, seg_sites = 100, qtl_per_chr = 20, plot_h2 = 0.3)
)
spec
```

`sim_replicates()` makes the replicate seeds, and `fit_resamples()` runs the
spec once on each. `collect_metrics()` gives the mean over replicates and its
Monte Carlo standard error:

```{r}
res <- fit_resamples(spec, sim_replicates(10, seed = 1), metrics = sim_metric_set(sim_metric("gain", "maximize")))
collect_metrics(res)
collect_metrics(res, summarize = FALSE)
```

`sim_metric("gain", "maximize")` names an outcome your function returns and
says which direction is better. The direction is used when ranking designs.

Inside your function `SP` is also set globally while it runs, so AlphaSimR
functions work with or without `simParam = SP`. Scripts copied from the
AlphaSimR documentation run unchanged.

## Step 4: compare designs with `tune()`

Mark the setting you want to compare with `tune()`, and give `tune_grid()`
the values to try:

```{r}
spec <- alphasim_program(
  recurrent,
  n_select = tune(),
  founders = asr_founders(n_founders = 50, n_chr = 5, seg_sites = 100, qtl_per_chr = 20, plot_h2 = 0.3)
)
res <- tune_grid(spec, sim_replicates(10, seed = 1), grid = data.frame(n_select = c(2, 5, 10, 20, 40)),
                 metrics = sim_metric_set(sim_metric("gain", "maximize")))
collect_metrics(res)
```

```{r, fig.alt = "Mean gain after five cycles against the number of selected parents, with error bars."}
autoplot(res)
```

Every design ran on the same ten founder populations, with the same random
numbers. Differences between designs therefore come from the designs, not
from luck, which is why a handful of replicates already separates them. The
[replicates article](replicates.html) explains this in more detail.

You can also give `tune_grid()` a number instead of a data frame, such as
`grid = 8`. tidyagsim then picks eight values spread over the range given
in `params`, for example `params = list(n_select = sim_param(c(2, 40)))`.

## Step 5: record the program with a tracker

Short-term gain is only one outcome. Most studies also care about gain per
year, remaining diversity and cost, and want to see how the program
progresses year by year. `asr_tracker()` and `asr_summary()` do that
bookkeeping:

* `tracker <- asr_tracker(founders)` remembers the founders' mean and
  variance, so later gains are in founder genetic standard deviations.
* `tracker$record(pop, year = , cost = )` stores the population's mean,
  genetic variance and heterozygosity, and adds the cost spent that year. If
  you pass `released_lines = `, their value becomes the program's release
  gain.
* `asr_summary(tracker)` returns the standard outcomes: `release_gain`,
  `gain_per_year`, `genetic_variance`, `expected_heterozygosity`, `cost`,
  `gain_per_cost`, `years` and the yearly `trajectory`.

Here is the same program with a tracker, ten cycles, one cycle per year, and
a cost of 15 dollars a plot:

```{r}
recurrent <- function(founders, SP, n_select, cycles = 10) {
  tracker <- asr_tracker(founders)
  pop <- founders
  for (cycle in seq_len(cycles)) {
    pop <- setPheno(pop)
    parents <- selectInd(pop, n_select)
    pop <- randCross(parents, nCrosses = 100)
    tracker$record(pop, year = cycle, cost = nInd(pop) * 15)
  }
  asr_summary(tracker)
}

spec <- alphasim_program(recurrent, n_select = tune(),
                         founders = asr_founders(n_founders = 50, n_chr = 5, seg_sites = 100, qtl_per_chr = 20))
res <- tune_grid(spec, sim_replicates(10, seed = 1), grid = data.frame(n_select = c(2, 5, 10, 20, 40)),
                 control = control_sim(save_outcomes = TRUE))
collect_metrics(res, type = "wide")[, c("n_select", "release_gain", "genetic_variance", "cost")]
```

Without a `metrics` argument, an `alphasim_program()` reports
`release_gain`, `gain_per_year`, `genetic_variance` and `cost`. With
`control_sim(save_outcomes = TRUE)` the yearly records are kept, and
`collect_trajectories()` returns them:

```{r, fig.alt = "Mean genetic value over ten years for five numbers of selected parents. Two parents stall early, forty gain slowly, and five to twenty gain most."}
traj <- collect_trajectories(res)
avg <- aggregate(mean ~ n_select + year, data = traj, FUN = mean)
ggplot(avg, aes(year, mean, colour = factor(n_select))) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Year", y = "Mean genetic value (founder SDs)", colour = "Parents selected",
       title = "Too few parents stall, too many gain slowly")
```

## Step 6: report your own outcomes

Anything else you want to compare, pass to `asr_summary()` as an extra
argument. Then name it in the metric set. Here we add the accuracy of the
last round of selection and the genetic value of the single best plant:

```{r}
recurrent <- function(founders, SP, n_select, cycles = 10) {
  tracker <- asr_tracker(founders)
  pop <- founders
  for (cycle in seq_len(cycles)) {
    pop <- setPheno(pop)
    accuracy <- cor(pheno(pop)[, 1], gv(pop)[, 1])
    parents <- selectInd(pop, n_select)
    pop <- randCross(parents, nCrosses = 100)
    tracker$record(pop, year = cycle, cost = nInd(pop) * 15)
  }
  best <- (max(gv(pop)) - tracker$base$mean) / tracker$base$sd
  asr_summary(tracker, accuracy = accuracy, best_plant = best)
}

spec <- alphasim_program(recurrent, n_select = tune(),
                         founders = asr_founders(n_founders = 50, n_chr = 5, seg_sites = 100, qtl_per_chr = 20))
res <- tune_grid(spec, sim_replicates(10, seed = 1), grid = data.frame(n_select = c(5, 10, 40)),
                 metrics = sim_metric_set(release_gain, accuracy, sim_metric("best_plant", "maximize")))
collect_metrics(res, type = "wide")[, c("n_select", "release_gain", "accuracy", "best_plant")]
```

`accuracy` is a built-in metric, so its name is enough. `best_plant` is new,
so `sim_metric()` declares it. Selection accuracy falls as selection gets
stronger, because strongly selected populations lose genetic variance. (With
only two parents, the population becomes fixed within ten cycles, so
accuracy cannot even be computed. That is why this grid starts at five.)

## Step 7: assumptions, ranges and impossible designs

Three more arguments of `alphasim_program()` round it out.

**Assumptions as scenarios.** Every `asr_founders()` field, such as
`plot_h2` or `qtl_per_chr`, can also be set from the study. To see whether
the best design depends on heritability, run it under two scenarios:

```{r}
res <- tune_grid(spec, sim_replicates(10, seed = 1, scenarios = sim_scenarios(plot_h2 = c(0.1, 0.5))),
                 grid = data.frame(n_select = c(5, 10, 40)), metrics = sim_metric_set(release_gain))
collect_metrics(res, type = "wide")[, c(".scenario", "n_select", "release_gain", "release_gain_se")]
```

**Ranges.** `params` gives the range of each tuned setting, for generated
grids, `tune_race()` and `tune_bayes()`:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
spec <- alphasim_program(recurrent, n_select = tune(),
                         params = list(n_select = sim_param(c(2L, 60L), label = "Parents selected")))
res <- tune_bayes(spec, sim_replicates(10), initial = 5, iter = 10)
```

**Impossible designs.** `check` is a function of the settings that returns
`NULL` when a design can run, or a reason when it can't. tidyagsim skips
those designs and records the reason, which `collect_notes()` shows:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
spec <- alphasim_program(recurrent, n_select = tune(),
                         check = function(n_select) if (n_select > 100) "Only 100 plants per cycle.")
```

## Checklist

* The function starts with `founders, SP`, and returns a named list of single
  numbers (or `asr_summary()`).
* No `set.seed()` inside. Let the replicates do the seeding.
* Every setting you want to compare is an argument, and marked `tune()` in
  `alphasim_program()`.
* Extra traits, correlations or SNP chips go in `asr_founders(setup = )`,
  a function of `SP`. Your own marker data go in
  `asr_founders(haplotypes = )`.
* Long studies: `control_sim(parallel = TRUE)` runs designs in parallel, and
  `cache = "folder"` lets an interrupted study resume. `write_slurm_array()`
  writes the files for a computing cluster.
